papers.title: Structural latent dimension: deterministic geometry and local Fisher structure
papers.abstract: We study the structural dimension of a second-order object: the minimum latent dimension that remains necessary relative to a declared class of competing dependence. Building on minimum-rank factor analysis and low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, we use distances to lower-dimensional classes to describe inference near structural ambiguity. General distance and tangent-cone facts yield confidence statements and local margins. For rank-zero competitors with bounded residual degree, we derive exact maximum-weight $b$-matching formulas, support-slack tangent cones and sparse-spike angles; a shared residual support across a field can produce separation absent pointwise. We give positive-semidefinite brackets, a dimension-free Gaussian likelihood expansion, an exact quotient by the tangent of a low-rank background, and a detection floor from the margin. Equal-angle configurations with different branch multiplicities motivate static and spectral detection conjectures. Joint low-rank/residual profiling and the sharp composite information boundaries remain open.

papers.title: Sensor Monitoring Towards Industry 4.0: Bridging Concepts on the $C_n$ Multivariate Control Chart
papers.abstract: The main challenge in monitoring multiple sensors is the high dimensionality that a process can easily reach. From a decision-making perspective, converting these multivariate dynamics into an informative visualization is also not trivial. Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques detect changes in quality characteristics, but they are difficult to apply beyond the normality (Gaussian) assumption. For instance, the most well-known SPC multivariate control chart is based on Hotelling's $T^2$ statistic, which assumes that the process data follow a multivariate normal distribution (which rarely occurs in practice) and that the observations are serially independent. This study focuses on the multivariate case (dimension $d \geq 2$), regardless of the data dependence or marginal asymmetry. We propose a new control chart for change detection in copula-based multivariate processes, called the $C_n$-chart, which is based on a density level-set tolerance region built from a copula function, and we derive its run-length properties. The methodology also quantifies the (not necessarily linear) dependence among the variables. Two case studies are presented, one on water quality control and the other on monitoring brass-steel thermostats, complemented by a simulation study of run-length performance and computational cost. The results show that the proposed methodology captures both the association among variables and the anomalies, and that it accommodates variable selection through conditional (regression) modeling of the margins.

papers.title: Statistical methods for extrapolation from one population to another: a review
papers.abstract: Background: Extrapolation refers to statistical approaches that support inference on treatment effects in a target population using data from completed clinical trials conducted in a source population. This is particularly important when only limited data are available in the target population. Extrapolation may be based on multiple sources of information, including pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, mechanistic, or clinical outcome data. This review focuses on methods that enable borrowing of information from one population to support inference in another. Methods: We conducted a review of statistical methodologies for extrapolation, focusing on approaches that incorporate outcome data from source populations to support inference in target populations. Methods were identified across a range of settings, including extrapolation across age groups and across different clinical indications. Literature searches were conducted using the Science Citation Index Expanded database within Web of Science and included all English-language records available up to 30 June 2025. Results: The review identified 218 extrapolation approaches from 159 papers, which can be broadly classified into three main categories: Bayesian, frequentist, and causal inference methods. These methods vary in their assumptions, implementation, and applicability across different extrapolation settings. Conclusions: This review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of statistical methods for extrapolation, offering a foundation for further methodological development and applied research. It also discusses key considerations for method selection and current limitations, and highlights priorities for future research, including the development of new extrapolation methods and clinical trial designs that facilitate extrapolation.
